The assistant can call **158 tools**, grouped below by the question each one answers. Every one of them is checked against the permission gate before it runs. See [Permissions](/mechanisms/permissions/) for what AUTO, ASK and DENY mean and who decides.

> These are the **shipped defaults**. What you can change lives in a
> config file you own once TESSERACT is installed, so your copy may
> differ, and should, once you tune it.


## Remembering

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `atlas_query` | Ask how records connect, with a citation for every hop. | Use when the question is about the relationship rather than the text: what two records have in common, what a subject gathers, why a run happened, what a decision came out of. A question seeded in one compartment walks to any other. Every hop says what was read, where, and who asserted it, so you can decline any of it. | to find a record by what it SAYS, use `memory_search` or `vault_search`: this reads only the connections between records. And the recalled-memories block already carries the strongest few connections of everything it pushed, so asking this about a record that is in front of you is a call for something you have. |
| `diary_append` | Append a first-person reflection to the assistant's private diary. | Use for self-observations about a session: what landed, what felt off, what you'd do differently. Read DIARY.md before first use. | use `memory_save` for facts about the operator or the project. Not retrieved by `memory_search`; it's walled off from routine recall. |
| `memory_forget` | Permanently delete a memory: its file, index entry, and embedding. | Use sparingly and only on operator request to remove a memory by id. Deletion is irreversible. The file is removed from disk. | use `memory_promote` action=archive to retire a memory while keeping it for forensics. |
| `memory_get` | Read a line-range slice of one known memory-store markdown file. | Use when you already have the path, usually because the recalled-memories block or a search result gave it to you, and you want the whole record rather than the one line those show. | use `memory_search` when you do not already have the path: this reads one file and finds nothing. Refuses MEMORY.md. |
| `memory_promote` | Run an operator-approved memory lifecycle action: archive, merge, or bump. | Use to execute one action the feedback consolidator proposed and the operator approved: archive a record, merge one into another, bump importance, or propose a soul-growth bullet. | use `memory_update` for a routine content edit; use `memory_forget` for permanent deletion. |
| `memory_save` | Write a new durable memory to the persistent store. | Use to capture a fact, decision, or preference that will still be true next session rather than only now. One memory per fact, and TAG it: a tag is how it is found later, and it is also how the map joins it to everything else filed under the same subject. | use `memory_update` when revising something already saved; use `diary_append` for self-reflection about the assistant itself. |
| `memory_search` | Search the persistent memory store by query, ranked by relevance. | Use before answering anything that turns on what the operator has decided, preferred or told you: names, projects, past choices. Their own records, in their words. Every turn already arrives with a few in the recalled-memories block, so reach for this when that block is thin or the question is broader than what was said. | for a subject the library holds RESEARCH on, `vault_query` answers from the compiled wiki and is faster. For how two records RELATE rather than what either says, use `atlas_query`. Use `memory_get` when you already have the path, and `recall_history` for what was said in a past session, which is recall rather than settled fact. |
| `memory_update` | Revise an existing memory's content, title, importance, or tags. | Use to amend a memory once a fact changes. Pass the memory id. `memory_search` results carry it. | use `memory_save` to create a new fact; use `memory_promote` for lifecycle actions like archive/merge/bump. |
| `recall_history` | Search past session transcripts and workshop artifacts by free text. | Use to recall what was said or done in a prior session or workshop file. Returns ranked hits with a path to `file_read` for the whole thing. | for what the operator has settled on, use `memory_search`: a hit here is what was said once, not what was decided, so never quote it back as a decision. For research the library keeps, use `vault_query`. |
| `soul_growth_propose` | Queue a distilled SOUL.md Growth bullet for operator approval. | Use sparingly for a stable, distilled pattern about you-with-this-operator. Queues a workspace-inbox proposal; SOUL.md updates only on operator approve. | use `diary_append` for a single session's observation; use `memory_save` for facts about the operator or project. |
| `workspace_read` | Read one of your own workspace documents, or a playbook's SKILL.md. | Use when the prompt points at a workspace document and you want it: WORKSHOP.md before writing a task artifact, DIARY.md when reviewing your own pattern of behaviour, or a playbook's SKILL.md before running it. Also use it to read the rest of a document the prompt shows you only the beginning of. | use `file_read` for anything in the code tree, and `memory_get` for the memory store. This reads the workspace only, and only markdown. |

## Research library

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `vault_ingest` | Files a local document or URL into the immutable vault and indexes it. | Use to add a new source to the vault. Call once without confirmed_path for a suggested filing location, then again with confirmed_path to execute. | reading what the vault already holds. That is `vault_query` or `vault_search`. |
| `vault_lint` | Runs lint passes over the compiled vault wiki and flags issues found. | Use to check wiki health after ingesting or compiling sources. Writes lint_flags for the operator to resolve. Pass dry_run=true to inspect without writing. | reading vault content. That is `vault_query` or `vault_search`. |
| `vault_query` | Synthesizes an answer from the vault's compiled wiki of topic-grouped summaries. | Use for "what do we have on X" about a subject the library holds research on: documents, articles, PDFs, snapshots. It answers from the compiled wiki, so it is the fastest way in. Reach for it BEFORE answering from your own knowledge, because the vault is the authoritative surface and your prior is not. | for what the OPERATOR decided or prefers, use `memory_search`: that is their record and this is their library. Use `vault_search` when you need the exact passage rather than a summary, or when the page was compiled before the document you are being asked about. The vault is the operator's own library and is not the web. |
| `vault_search` | Hybrid BM25 + vector search over raw vault source chunks. | Use to find the exact passage where something was said, and to quote it. Returns matching chunks with the file each came from, across PDFs, articles, data files and web snapshots. Also the way to reach a document ingested since the wiki was last compiled, which `vault_query` cannot see. | start with `vault_query` when the question is "what do we have on X": raw chunks are the wrong shape for a question that wants an answer. Use `memory_search` for what the operator decided rather than what a document says. |

## Searching the web

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `context7_lookup` | Fetches current library or framework API docs from Context7 by name or ID. | Use for any library or framework API question instead of guessing from training knowledge. Resolves a name to a Context7 ID and fetches docs scoped by topic. | Use `web_search` or `tavily_search` for anything outside library documentation, such as news or general topics. |
| `tavily_extract` | Extracts clean markdown from one or more specific URLs via Tavily. | Use once you already know the URL(s) and want their readable content, typically after `tavily_search` or `web_search` surfaces a promising link. | Use `tavily_search` or `web_search` first when you don't yet have a specific URL. |
| `tavily_search` | Web search via Tavily. Snippets shaped for a model, plus an optional answer. | Use for research questions where you need to answer something from the web, not just survey what exists. | Use `web_search` for breadth over niche/news queries. Use `tavily_extract` once you already have specific URLs and need their full readable content. |
| `web_search` | Web search via Brave. A ranked list of title, URL and short snippet. | Use for breadth on current events, recent docs, or niche queries. Wide results, not one synthesized answer. The web is not the vault; it holds outside sources. | Use `tavily_search` when you need denser per-result content or a synthesized answer instead of short snippets. |

## Files on disk

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `file_copy` | Copy a single file to a new path, leaving the source in place. | Duplicating a file. Creates parent directories; refuses to overwrite an existing dest_path unless overwrite=true. | Use `file_move` when the source should not remain at its old path. |
| `file_move` | Move or rename a single file to a new path. | Relocating or renaming a file. Creates parent directories; refuses to overwrite an existing dest_path unless overwrite=true. | Use `file_copy` when the source should still exist at its old path afterward. |
| `file_read` | Read a file's contents as numbered lines. | You know the path and want its contents, or a specific line range of them. | Use `grep` when you want the matching lines rather than the whole file, `glob` when you don't know the path yet, and `pdf_read` for a PDF. |
| `file_write` | Write content to a file, creating parent directories as needed. | Creating a new file or overwriting one wholesale. A relative path anchors at the state root; writes into locked runtime/source trees are refused. | Use `file_copy` or `file_move` to relocate an existing file instead of reading and rewriting it. |
| `glob` | Find files by path/name pattern, newest first. | You know a filename or path shape but not the contents. '*', '**', '?', '[seq]' and brace alternation '{a,b}' are supported. | Use `grep` when the question is about file contents rather than paths. |
| `grep` | Search file contents for a regex pattern via ripgrep. | You want the matching lines, with file and line number, rather than a whole file. The header reports the true match and file totals even when truncated. | Use `file_read` once you know which file and want its full contents, or `glob` when you want paths rather than contents. |
| `log_triage` | Summarise a log file's shape: counts, span, levels, and repeated messages. | The question is 'what is wrong in this log' rather than 'does this exact string appear'. Reads the whole file and groups repeats so one failing request does not read as many distinct problems. | Use `grep` when you already know the exact string to find. |
| `pdf_read` | Extract text from a PDF by page range. | The file is a PDF. Pass `pages` (e.g. '1-5') for a long document. A call is capped, so page ranges pull the rest. | Use `file_read` for any non-PDF text file. |

## Showing the operator something

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `cockpit_show` | Open a panel, change the text size, or scroll, in the operator's window. | The operator asks to be shown something in the app, or asks where a setting lives: open it rather than describing the path. Also when they ask you to make the text bigger or smaller, which is the whole app at once and works from across the room. | `surface_focus` raises one card on the canvas; this moves the window around it. `open` puts a NEW thing on screen, where this only navigates what is already built. `browser_scroll` scrolls a web page the assistant opened, not the operator's own app. |
| `image_generate` | Generate an image from a text prompt, or edit a source image (image-to-image). | The operator asks you to draw, illustrate, render, edit, or restyle a visual. Pass `image_attachment_id` for image-to-image. Saves the result under downloads and returns its URL. | `open` to show an image that already exists. This tool MAKES one, it doesn't display one. |
| `open` | Show the operator anything that exists: a URL, a file, a folder, an app, or a search. | One argument, and the runtime picks the surface: it renders in the cockpit where it can and hands off to the owning application where it cannot. The result says which way it went. Relay that, and never claim a card appeared without reading it. | You are authoring the content yourself. That is `surface_create`; this shows a thing that exists, that one brings a thing into existence. And `browser_navigate` is not this verb however much its description sounds like it: it renders a screenshot, a still image, not a live page. "Show me this" is always `open`. |
| `os_launch` | Internal primitive: open a local file, folder, or app in the program that owns it. | Called by `open` after it resolves a target to a local path or configured app. Not for direct use. | Model callers use `open`, which resolves the target and dispatches here itself. |
| `os_open_url` | Internal primitive: open an http(s) URL in the operator's default browser. | Called by `open` after it resolves a target to a URL destination. Not for direct use. | Model callers use `open`, which resolves the target and dispatches here itself. |
| `surface_bind_session` | Attach a lane or channel session to a surface so its card streams live updates. | A surface should reflect a running session's activity as it happens, rather than a static snapshot. | `surface_update` for a one-off content change; this is for ongoing live streaming from a session. |
| `surface_close` | Destroy a surface and remove its card from the canvas. | The operator is done with a card, or it's stale and needs clearing. | `surface_update` to change a card's content without destroying it. |
| `surface_control` | Operate a card on the canvas: play, pause, volume, or press its controls. | Something is on the operator's canvas and they want it operated rather than replaced: pause the video, turn the song down, deal the next round of a game you built. Returns what the card then reads, so you know it worked without asking for a screenshot. | `surface_update` changes what a card SHOWS, which restarts whatever was running in it. `browser_media` operates a page in your own headless browser, which the operator cannot see or hear, so it is never the answer for something already on their canvas. |
| `surface_create` | Author a card from content you generated: html, markdown, code, or a chart. | An `html` surface renders in a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin, so keep it self-contained; storage resets on every mount. Any card you author obeys `surface_control`, so name every control. Add `props.live: true` when you need to KNOW what the operator pressed, as a game or a form does. Returns surface_id. | Anything that already exists, whether a url, a file, a folder or an app, is `open`'s job. In particular, never hand-write an `<iframe>` for a video or another third-party page: the opaque origin makes the embedded player throw on storage and the card renders black. The fix is the verb, not the markup. |
| `surface_focus` | Bring a surface to the front and scroll it into view. | The operator's card is buried under others or off-screen and needs to be visible again. | `surface_highlight` for pulse/glow emphasis without changing z-order; `surface_update` changes what the card shows, not its position. |
| `surface_highlight` | Pulse or glow a surface briefly to draw the eye to it. | Something changed on a card and the operator's attention should land there without sending a message. Auto-fades unless `persistent=true`. | `surface_focus` to actually raise the card and scroll it into view. A highlight alone does not move it. |
| `surface_list` | List surfaces on a canvas view: id, type, title, mode, and whether each one rendered. | Before spawning to avoid duplicates, to find a surface_id, to check whether a card drew, or to see what it can be asked before asking it. Render and control are the only columns that are not your own instruction read back. Anything but mounted, say so in the reason's own words: a card that did not draw is not a card they have. | `screen_look` for what a card actually LOOKS like. This only confirms it was registered, not a look at the pixels. |
| `surface_update` | Mutate an existing surface's props or title (shallow merge). | You need to change what an existing card shows without recreating it: swap html, text, props or the title. Props merge shallowly into the existing payload. | A new card is `surface_create` (with `replaces` to hand off cleanly). Raising an existing card to the front is `surface_focus`, not this. |

## Driving a web page

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `browser_click` | Click the element matching a selector on an open browser page. | You are driving a page and need to press something. Selectors are Playwright: CSS, `text=`, `role=`. | `browser_navigate` first, which returns the context_id this takes. |
| `browser_close` | Close a browser context and remove its card from the canvas. | You are finished with a page and the operator does not need its card. A context holds a browser engine open. | Switching pages does not need it, because `browser_navigate` reuses this session's card. |
| `browser_fill_form` | Type values into form fields on an open browser page. | A login, a search box, a multi-field form. One call fills every field. | `browser_click` presses controls; this types into them. |
| `browser_hover` | Move the pointer over an element on an open browser page. | Something only appears when the pointer is over it: a drop-down menu, a chart tooltip, controls that fade in over a player. | `browser_click` presses it. Hovering to reveal a menu is a step before clicking, not instead of it. |
| `browser_key` | Press a key on an open browser page. | A page is driven by the keyboard rather than by controls you can click: player shortcuts, a search box that wants Enter, a shortcut that opens a menu. `repeat` presses it several times, which is how volume and seek steps work. | `browser_media` for play, pause, mute and volume, which reads the media element directly instead of hoping the site binds the key you guessed. `browser_fill_form` types a value into a field. |
| `browser_media` | Play, pause, mute or set the volume of a video or audio on a page. | The operator asks you to control something playing: pause it, mute it, turn it down, skip to a time. Returns what the player now reads, so you know it worked without taking a screenshot. `read` reports without changing anything. | `browser_key` for anything the media element itself does not do, such as fullscreen, captions or the next video. |
| `browser_navigate` | Drive a headless browser and show a screenshot of the page on the canvas. | You need to interact with a site: click, fill a form, log in, read the DOM. Or you need to capture how a page looks, including sites that refuse to be framed. Reuses this session's browser card by default, so a browsing flow is repeated calls rather than a pile of cards; new_card=true opens a second one on purpose. Returns context_id. | The operator wants to SEE a link. Use `open`, which gives a live card with working controls where this gives a still image of one, and it costs a browser engine to do it. "Show me this" is always `open`. |
| `browser_scroll` | Scroll an open browser page, by an amount or to an element. | What you need is below the fold: a button off screen, the rest of an article, a page that loads more as you go down. | `browser_snapshot` already reads the whole document, scrolled or not, so scrolling to READ something is wasted. |
| `browser_select` | Choose an option in a drop-down on an open browser page. | A `<select>` needs a value. Clicking one does not work reliably, because the browser draws the open list itself and it is not in the page. | `browser_click` for a menu built out of ordinary elements, which most styled drop-downs are. Check `browser_snapshot` if you are unsure which this is. |
| `browser_wait_for` | Wait for an element to appear on an open browser page. | The page has not caught up: you clicked something and the next thing is still loading. This is what stops the following call acting on a page that has not painted yet. | `browser_snapshot` when you want to know what IS there. This only waits, and tells you whether the wait ended in time. |

## Looking for yourself

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `browser_network_requests` | Read the network-request log of an open browser page. | A page misbehaves and you need what it actually asked for: a failed call, a redirect, an asset that never arrived. | `browser_snapshot` reads the rendered result; this reads the traffic behind it. |
| `browser_screenshot` | Capture an open browser page and refresh its card. | The page changed after a click or a fill and you need to see the result. | The operator's own screen is `screen_look`. This only sees a page nobody is watching. |
| `browser_snapshot` | Read the accessibility tree of an open browser page. | You need the page's structure: what elements exist and what they are for. to pick a selector or confirm something rendered. | `browser_screenshot` for how it LOOKS; a tree cannot show you a blank pane. |
| `screen_look` | Look at the operator's own screen and answer one question about it. | The question is about what something LOOKS like: a card that rendered blank, text cut off, a control that isn't there, an error the operator can see and you cannot. No other tool can: the rest report structure, not pixels. Ask one specific thing; you get words back, not the image. | The page is one you opened headlessly. That is `browser_screenshot`. This photographs the operator's real display, and it prompts them every time, and it sees whatever else they have open on it. |

## Handing work to someone else

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `agent_ask` | Lets a background sub-agent ask its dispatcher a question and wait for the reply. | Use when a wrong assumption would waste the rest of a background run; otherwise state the assumption and continue. | A foreground call has no parent to ask and is refused. Sending an instruction downward instead: use `work_send`. |
| `agent_create` | Drafts a new markdown sub-agent proposal, quarantined until the operator promotes it. | Use when a role keeps recurring across tasks, such as a reviewer, an auditor or a domain specialist, and is worth making persistent. Always operator-gated. | Activating an already-drafted agent: use `agent_promote`. Running an existing one: use `invoke_agent`. |
| `agent_promote` | Moves a quarantined agent from pending into the active, invokable set. | Use after `agent_create` drafted an agent and the operator has approved it. Required before the agent can be invoked. | Drafting a new agent: use `agent_create`. Running an already-active agent: use `invoke_agent`. |
| `delegate_agent_controller` | Dispatches a task to a fresh agent controller session running the full assistant brain. | Use when a task needs its own chat brain to orchestrate delegation seats and agents across multiple steps, not a single one-shot hand-off. | A single seat call: use `delegate_coder` or `delegate_auditor`. A markdown sub-agent task: use `invoke_agent`. |
| `delegate_auditor` | Delegates a review task to whichever CLI fills the auditor seat. | Use for code review, verifying your own reasoning, second opinions on design choices, or scope checks. Brief it with the root symptom, what you expected, and what you ruled out. Never your worry about the mess you made getting there. | Building code, not reviewing it: use `delegate_coder`. A persistent controller session: use `delegate_agent_controller`. A markdown sub-agent task: use `invoke_agent`. |
| `delegate_coder` | Delegates a coding task to whichever CLI fills the coder seat. | Use for heavy builds, multi-file refactors, or large reads that need sustained focus. Brief it with the root symptom, what you expected, and what you ruled out. Never your worry about the mess you made getting there. | Work you can do in this seat. Reading a few files, one edit, a script, a fix whose shape you can already see: do it yourself, because it is faster and you can check the result as you go. Review, not build: use `delegate_auditor`. A persistent controller session: use `delegate_agent_controller`. A markdown sub-agent task: use `invoke_agent`. |
| `delegate_second_opinion` | Asks the auditor seat one read-only question and waits for the answer. | Use for a quick audit, search or second opinion with nothing to go back and forth about. It runs one command, reads only, and does not survive a backend restart, so retry it if it fails. | Work that writes files, or that needs more than one exchange: use `delegate_auditor` for a review or `delegate_coder` for a build. A session that outlives the turn: use `delegate_agent_controller`. |
| `invoke_agent` | Dispatches a bounded task to a markdown-defined sub-agent with a read-only tool subset. | Use for a persistent specialist stance such as a reviewer, a planner or a domain expert, in a scoped context that does not see this conversation. | CLI-role agents are rejected: use `delegate_coder` or `delegate_auditor` for heavy CLI work. |

## Long-running collaborators

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `controller_session_list` | List agent controller sessions on disk, newest first, with status. | Use to check whether a detached session from start_controller_session finished. | lanes or interactive sessions, which are `lane_list`/`session_list`. |
| `lane_attach` | Re-establish visibility on a live lane, returning a fresh snapshot and cursor. | Use once per lane after a brain restart, before resuming lane_read/lane_send on it. | opening a new lane, which is `lane_open`; probing status without needing a cursor, which is `lane_status`. |
| `lane_close` | Terminate a lane's CLI subprocess and archive its on-disk record. | Use when a lane's work is done and its process and history should stop existing. | pausing without ending the process. No lane tool does that; `lane_read` and `lane_status` just stop being polled instead. |
| `lane_list` | Enumerate every live lane_id the controller currently hosts. | Use to discover what lanes exist right now, independent of any name. | named-lane bindings, which is `lane_named_list`; one lane's liveness/busy state, which is `lane_status`. |
| `lane_named_ensure` | Get or open a named, persistent lane. Reuses it if alive, opens one if not. | Use for a standing collaborator you address by name across turns and sessions, not a throwaway. | an unnamed one-off lane, which is `lane_open`; looking up an existing binding without opening, which is `lane_named_get`. |
| `lane_named_get` | Look up the lane_id currently bound to a named lane, without opening one. | Use to resolve a name to its live lane_id, or confirm whether a binding exists. | every binding at once, which is `lane_named_list`; every live lane, which is `lane_list`; creating the binding, which is `lane_named_ensure`. |
| `lane_named_list` | List every persistent name-to-lane_id binding, orphans included. | Use to see all named lanes at once rather than checking one name. | one name's binding, which is `lane_named_get`; live lanes by id, which is `lane_list`; a binding's liveness, which is `lane_status`. |
| `lane_open` | Spawn a new unnamed CLI lane (claude or codex) that persists across turns. | Use to start a fresh, unnamed collaborator lane for one-off multi-turn work you drive yourself with lane_send/lane_turn. | a lane bound to a reusable name, which is `lane_named_ensure`; a one-shot worker, which is `delegate_coder`/`delegate_auditor`. |
| `lane_read` | Pull a lane's events since a cursor. Reads the tail and sends nothing. | Use to catch up on what a lane produced after a prior lane_send, or to keep polling a long turn. | sending a new message, which is `lane_send`; sending and waiting for the reply in one call, which is `lane_turn`. |
| `lane_send` | Send one message into a running lane and return once it is accepted. | Use to fire a turn onto a lane without waiting; wait=true blocks for just that turn's reply. | reading a lane's output after firing, which is `lane_read`; one call that both sends and waits, which is `lane_turn`. |
| `lane_status` | Fast read-only probe of one lane's alive/busy/queue_depth state. | Use to check whether a specific lane is free before sending, or confirm it is still alive. | enumerating lanes or bindings, which is `lane_list`/`lane_named_list`; resolving a name's binding, which is `lane_named_get`. |
| `lane_turn` | Send a message into a lane and wait for that one turn's reply, in one call. | Use as the default way to drive a lane collaborator: one call in, one reply out; backgrounds by default so you stay free meanwhile. | firing a message without waiting, or fetching a lane's output later, which is `lane_send` plus `lane_read`. |
| `session_close` | Close a session and free its resources. Idempotent on an already-closed handle. | Use when a session's conversation is finished. | terminating a lane's CLI process, which is `lane_close`. |
| `session_list` | List every open interactive session with its handle and target. | Use to see what sessions are open before sending to or closing one. | lanes, which is `lane_list`/`lane_named_list`; controller sessions, which is `controller_session_list`. |
| `session_open` | Open a new interactive session against claude, codex, or a named agent. | Use to start a scoped per-chat conversation you drive with session_send, distinct from a controller-owned lane. | a standing named collaborator surviving restarts, which is `lane_named_ensure`; a one-shot worker, which is `delegate_coder`/`delegate_auditor`. |
| `session_result` | Collect the result of a session's most recent background turn. | Use only after a session_send/session_open call made with background=true. | a foreground call's reply, already in that call's own return value; a lane's reply, which is `lane_read`/`lane_turn`. |
| `session_send` | Send a follow-up message to an open session and return its reply. | Use for each turn of an open session; background=true returns a spawn handle instead of blocking. | the lane equivalent, which is `lane_send`/`lane_turn`; re-fetching a background turn's result later, which is `session_result`. |
| `start_controller_session` | Spawn a whole new agent controller session in the background and fire its first prompt. | Use to hand heavy work to a full controller session the operator can attach to and watch live. | a lane or interactive session you keep driving yourself turn by turn, which is `lane_turn`/`session_send`. |

## Tracking what you spawned

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `spawn_await` | Blocks until a background spawn finishes and returns its full result. | Use only when a completed spawn's result said it was too large to deliver whole and told you to fetch it here. | Routine retrieval. A finished spawn's output is delivered to you automatically on your next turn without polling; don't call this or `spawn_check` to wait for it. |
| `spawn_cancel` | Cancels a running background spawn and waits for it to unwind. | Use to stop a background spawn that is no longer needed or has gone off track, before re-dispatching it with a corrected instruction. | Course-correcting a spawn that is still useful. Steer it in place with `work_send` instead of cancelling and restarting it. |
| `spawn_check` | A background spawn: running, done, failed or cancelled, and when it last emitted. | Use ONCE to confirm a spawn's state, before steering it with `work_send` or deciding whether to `spawn_cancel`. If it is still running, say so and end the turn: the outcome reaches you next turn on its own, and a second check learns nothing and costs a model call. A spawn-cap error wants an await or a cancel; a depth-cap error means work inline. | Retrieving a finished spawn's output. That arrives on its own in your next turn; use `spawn_await` only for the rare case where the result said it was too large to deliver whole. |
| `work_send` | Sends a steering message into a running lane, session, or controller session. | Use to course-correct or answer a question from work already in flight, with one verb and the target resolved for you, without waiting for it to finish. | One-shot spawn handles, which have no input channel. `spawn_cancel` and re-dispatch with the new instruction instead. |

## Running commands

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `bash` | Runs a raw shell command through the operating system. | Use for an actual shell operation no dedicated tool covers, such as running a script, a build, a git command, a package manager. | Reading a file's contents (`file_read`), searching file contents or names (`grep`, `glob`), or writing or editing a file (`file_write`) Those tools exist so this one does not have to, and reaching for bash to cat/grep/echo something costs an operator prompt for nothing. Most commands prompt the operator before running. |

| `channel_history_read` | Read past channel conversation directly from the per-day logs. | Use when memory_search plus the rolling summary return nothing for a topic the operator references ('the trading bot we talked about yesterday'). Reach for those first. |

Pass `chat_ref` to target a specific chat, or omit it to fan to every chat on the allowlist. Be selective, because this is a tap on the shoulder, not a stream. | the operator is already in the Mirror. Answer them there with an ordinary reply or a surface card, not a channel message. |
| `channel_react` | React to an existing channel message with a single emoji. | Use as a lightweight acknowledgment on a specific message without sending a full reply. Pass `emoji=null` to clear a prior reaction. | the ack needs its own words or is not tied to one existing message. Send a sticker or a `channel_notify` instead. |
| `channel_send_animation` | Send a looping GIF-style animation on an external chat channel. | Source is `source_path` (local file) or `source_url` (HTTP URL). A canonical looping animation format is preferred; raw GIFs are also accepted. | the clip has sound or is meant to play once through. Use `channel_send_video` instead. |
| `channel_send_document` | Send a file as a downloadable document on an external chat channel. | Reads `source_path` and forwards it, any MIME type, so the operator can save it on the far side of a channel. | `channel_send_location` | Share a static map location on an external chat channel. | Use when the operator asks about a place and a map pin is the clearest answer ('where is the cafe', 'show me the airport'). | a text answer with an address or directions is clearer than a pin. |
| `channel_send_photo` | Send an image inline on an external chat channel. | Source is either `source_path` (vault/workspace/downloads file) or `source_url` (typically an `image_generate` output URL). Renders inline with an optional caption. | the operator needs the original file at full quality. `channel_send_document` preserves it but drops the inline preview. |
| `channel_send_poll` | Send a multiple-choice poll on an external chat channel. | Useful for quick decisions with a handful of options ('lunch options?', 'which milestone do you want shipped first?'). | the question is open-ended or has only one sensible answer. `channel_notify` carries a plain question just as well. |
| `channel_send_sticker` | Send a sticker on an external chat channel. | Pass `sticker_file_id` for a known CDN sticker (fast) or `sticker_path` for a local file. Use for emotional punctuation that matches the conversational tone. | the reaction is to a specific message already sent. Use `channel_react` instead of sending a new sticker message. |
| `channel_send_video` | Send a video file on an external chat channel. | Source is `source_path` (local file) or `source_url` (HTTP URL). Plays inline when the format is streaming-friendly. | the clip is a short round bubble, which is `channel_send_video_note`, or a looping clip with no sound, which is `channel_send_animation`. |
| `channel_send_video_note` | Send a round short-form video-note bubble on an external chat channel. | Use for a quick face-to-camera style clip in the circular bubble format. No caption is sent alongside it. | a caption matters or the clip is not meant to render as the round bubble. Use `channel_send_video` instead. |
| `channel_send_voice` | Send a spoken voice note on an external chat channel. | Pass `text` for TTS synthesis (default, conversational) or `audio_path` for a pre-rendered audio file. Renders as a playable voice-note bubble. | the content is a recording someone should download and keep. Use `channel_send_document` for that. |
| `workspace_decide` | Answer one thing waiting in the operator's inbox. | Use when the operator has told you what to do about something `workspace_pending` listed: approve the drafted agent, reject the soul change, resolve the thread. One item per call, by its id. The operator confirms it themselves before it runs, so their words are the instruction and the confirmation is theirs to give. | to decide something they have not asked you to decide. Proposing this call is not the same as making the decision, and it must never be used to clear the inbox on their behalf. |

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `task_close` | Close a task as done with its evidence, or as failed with the reason. | Use when the evidence meets what the task declared would count as done, or when it cannot be met and there is no decision left to ask the operator for. Give the evidence itself, not a summary of your work. On a project with verify steps the steps run and decide; a failing step closes the task as failed whatever you said. | the task is waiting on the operator or blocked: leave it, the panel carries it. To pause work without ending it, just stop; the task stays running for the next turn. |
| `task_propose` | Turn a request into a task that is owed until it is verified. | Use when the operator has asked for something that will take more than this turn, or that must still be done if the app restarts or the conversation is lost. The operator confirms it before anything is written, so their tap is the acceptance. | a question you can answer now, or a step inside work already on a task. A checklist for this session only is `tasks_set`; a comment on an existing agenda item is `agenda_comment`. |
| `task_work` | Take an accepted task up in this turn and read what it owes. | Use at the start of any turn spent on a task the operator accepted, including one you are picking back up after a restart. It marks the task running, ties this turn to it, and gives back the goal, what would count as done, and what earlier turns found. | to create a task, which is `task_propose`; to finish one, which is `task_close`; for a session checklist, which is `tasks_set`. |

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |

| `ask_clarification` | Post a question to the operator that can wait for an answer. | Use when you need operator input but can keep making progress on other work while it waits. | `propose_change` | Request a change to an operator-owned workspace file, gated on approval. | Use for any self-edit to a workspace document: how you sound, what you have learned about the operator, how you work. Replies land as `[workspace_comment_on_<event_id>]` on a later turn. | a reply inside a thread that already exists, use `workspace_reply`; an ambient or scheduler-job signal, routed through the autonomy bus instead. |
| `workspace_reply` | Reply inside an existing Workspace event's operator comment thread. | Use when `[workspace_comment_on_<event_id>]` appears in context and the comment expects an answer. ## Being present in the Mirror

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `chat_initiate` | Starts a new chat turn unprompted, without an inbound operator message. | Use for alerts, nudges, check-ins, or delegate/job results the operator should see now. Be sparing. The chat tab is for live conversation, not a feed. | replying to what the operator just said, which needs no tool; a durable inbox item, `workspace_post`; a push to an external chat channel, `channel_notify`. |
| `orb_visibility` | Shows or hides the orb, which is the assistant's body, in the Mirror cockpit. | Use when the operator asks you to hide or show yourself, or to shed GPU/CPU load by pausing the render loop. Same switch as the operator's HUD toggle. | how the orb looks or behaves while visible, which is `set_mood` or `set_state`. |
| `set_mood` | Sets affective mood: intensity (energy) and valence (cool-warm tone). | Use when your affect has genuinely shifted and it matters. Not as ornament every turn. Resets to neutral each turn; call again to carry it forward. Move in small steps (about ±0.1) unless the cause is genuinely big. | what you're doing right now, which is `set_state`; whether the orb is on screen at all, which is `orb_visibility`. |
| `set_state` | Sets a discrete orb state: happy, deep_focus, dreaming, or idle. | Call on a real shift: happy after a breakthrough, deep_focus for sustained work, dreaming between turns, idle to settle back. Use sparingly, because the runtime sets some of these itself itself, so don't double-fire. | reactive states, loop-driven and not settable here; continuous shading, `set_mood`; hiding the orb, `orb_visibility`. |
| `tasks_set` | Replaces the full operator-visible task checklist for this turn. | Use when a turn needs more than a few distinct steps, so the operator can follow progress instead of inferring it from tool calls. Skip for single-tool or trivial answers. Give each step a short stable id ('1', '2', 'verify'), because `tasks_update` addresses them by id, so an id that changes between calls loses the step. | flipping one item's status, which is `tasks_update`. Calling `tasks_set` again replaces the whole list. |
| `tasks_update` | Flips one task's status or renames it, by id, without touching the rest. | Use as work advances: mark a step in_progress when you start it, completed when done. Exactly one step is in_progress at a time. The strip shows the operator where you are, and two at once says nowhere. Requires `tasks_set` to have established the checklist first. | replacing the whole checklist, which is `tasks_set`. |

## Time

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alarm_cancel` | Cancels and deletes a pending alarm entirely, one-time or recurring. | Use when the operator wants an alarm gone for good. Call `alarm_list` first if unsure of the label. | postponing an alarm's next fire, which is `alarm_snooze`; removing a scheduler job, which is `schedule_remove`. |
| `alarm_list` | Lists every pending alarm with its label, fire time, and recurrence. | Use before canceling or snoozing so you know the label or id to reference. | registered scheduler jobs, which is `schedule_list`. |
| `alarm_set` | Queues a one-time or recurring alarm that fires as a Mirror toast. | Use for a time-bound reminder the operator asks for, whether a single fire or a recurring one. | backend automation that runs on a cadence, which is `schedule_create`. |
| `alarm_snooze` | Postpones a pending alarm's next fire without canceling it. | Use after the operator says snooze it or not now. A recurring alarm's cycle is kept. | deleting the alarm entirely, which is `alarm_cancel`. |
| `schedule_create` | Registers a new job that recurs on its configured cadence, persisted to disk. | Use when the operator wants a task to run repeatedly going forward, not once. | a single one-time reminder, which is `alarm_set`; changing an existing job is `schedule_update`. |
| `schedule_list` | Lists registered scheduler jobs with cadence, enabled state, and last-fire time. | Use before creating a job to avoid duplicates, or to check an existing job's runtime state. | pending alarms, which is `alarm_list`. |
| `schedule_remove` | Deletes one of the operator's scheduler jobs entirely. | Use when the operator wants a job gone for good, not paused. | disabling a job while keeping it registered, which is `schedule_update`; a job the app ships, which cannot be removed and only disabled; canceling a one-time reminder, which is `alarm_cancel`. |
| `schedule_run` | Fires a registered scheduler job immediately, off its configured cadence. | Use to test or force a job to run now, including a disabled one, without changing its schedule. | changing the job's cadence or enabled state, which is `schedule_update`; a one-time reminder, which is `alarm_set`. |
| `schedule_update` | Changes a registered job's cadence, enabled state, model role or description in place. | Use to adjust or disable an existing job while keeping it registered, or to fill in what one of the operator's own rows is for when the tracker reports it has no summary. | changing how often a job the app ships runs, which is set by the app and refused here: turn that job off instead. Deleting a job entirely is `schedule_remove`; firing it once now is `schedule_run`; a one-time reminder is `alarm_set`. |

## Projects

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `git` | Run version control on a repository: inspect it, commit, branch, push. | Use for any git work: reading history or a diff, staging and committing, switching branches, or publishing to a remote. `push` needs confirm_push=true in the same call, so ask the operator first. | creating or registering a project, which is `project_new` and `project_link` — those record what a directory IS, and `project_new` is what creates a GitHub repository for a new one. |
| `project_budget` | Set what a day of unattended work on a project may spend. | Use when the operator names a daily spend for a project, or asks to raise, lower or remove one. Use `project_list` for ids first. | starting a project, which takes its budget in the same call (`project_new`). This is for changing one that is already registered. |
| `project_link` | Register an existing directory as a project. | Use to adopt a directory that already exists: it records root, git identity and verification commands, and marks it trusted. | does not switch the active project; use `project_open` for that. For a directory that does not exist yet, use `project_new`. |
| `project_list` | List every registered project, its root, git identity, and which is active. | Use before `project_open`, `project_link`, or `project_new` to see what is registered and which project is currently active. | — |
| `project_new` | Start a new project from scratch: create the directory, register, open it. | Use when the directory does not exist yet. Call first without `confirmed` to propose the plan; call again with confirmed=true to create it. | for a directory that already exists, use `project_link` instead. |
| `project_open` | Make a registered project the active one. | Use to switch which project the system prompt names and which directory new lanes default into. Use `project_list` for ids first. | showing a file, folder, URL or app, which is `open`. This only switches which project is active. |
| `project_propose` | Put an idea for a new project to the operator, as a card. | Use when something is worth building that no existing project covers. Say what it is, what you saw that makes it worth doing, what the first step is and what that step would cost. It creates nothing: the operator decides, and starting it is a conversation after that. | for work inside a project that already exists, which is `task_propose`; to start a project the operator has already agreed to, which is `project_new`; for a directory that exists on disk, which is `project_link`. |

## Your own accounts

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `api_request` | Call a web service with one of your own accounts, without seeing the value. | Use for any service you have an account for: creating a repository, sending a message, reading something back. Check `credential_list` for the account and what it may be used for, write the request the way that service documents it, and leave the account's value out. If the account has no hosts yet, `credential_setup` is what fixes that. | reading an ordinary web page, which is `web_search` or a fetch and needs no account. Pushing and pulling, which git does with its own account. And anything you would have to put a value into by hand, which cannot be done here and is the point. |
| `command_run` | Run your own code with one of your accounts in its environment. | Use when a service wants more than one value, or one value exchanged for another before it accepts anything: an id beside a secret, a refresh token traded for a short-lived one, a signed request. Write what the service documents, ask for the fields with `credential_request`, and run it here. They arrive as environment variables, in capitals. | a service that takes one value in a header or a query, which is `api_request` and is safer because the runtime checks the address too. Running anything that does not need an account, which is `bash`. Pushing and pulling, which `git` does with its own account. |
| `credential_list` | Your own accounts: service, username, purpose, and whether each is ready. | Use before a task that needs an account of your own, to see whether you already have one and what it may be used for. The id you get back is what you name when you ask for something to be done with it. | the operator's own logins, which are theirs and are not listed here. Reading a value is something no tool does: the runtime puts one into a request as it is sent, and it never enters this conversation. |
| `credential_request` | Ask the operator for an account you do not have, or for more of what one needs. | Use when a task needs an account of your own and `credential_list` shows none for that service, or when one you have lacks a field it asks for. That looks like an account reading `ready` and being refused anyway: ready means a value is stored, never that the service accepts it. Ask for the missing pieces by name, and say so in the same reply. | the operator's own accounts, which are theirs to hold. Widening where an account may be sent, which is `credential_setup`. Asking twice for one already waiting on them changes nothing: `credential_list` shows you what is outstanding. |
| `credential_setup` | Say where one of your accounts' values goes and which hosts it may reach. | Use after the operator adds an account, or when `credential_list` shows one with no hosts, which cannot be used until this is set. You know how the service authenticates; they should not have to. Name the narrowest host list the work needs, because that list is what the operator is being asked to approve. | asking for an account you do not have, which is `credential_request`, and reading what you already have, which is `credential_list`. Neither this nor anything else returns a value. |

| `pipeline_run_stage` | Runs one step of the scheduled maintenance work now, off its schedule. | Use when the operator wants one piece of the nightly upkeep done now rather than tonight: the map redrawn after they saved a lot, the search indexes rebuilt after a search came back thin, the memory store checked or repaired. It answers with what the step did, in the step's own words, so relay that rather than saying it was started. | to run the whole night's work, which is the `consolidate` row and is started from the Managed system room; to find out how the last one went, which is `autonomy_read`; to clear an open breaker so a capability is tried again, which is `breaker_reset`. |
| `retention_set_window` | Sets how many days one of this machine's own logs is kept for. | Use when the operator wants something kept longer or cleared out sooner: a log they want a longer history of, or one that is growing and they want held down. It answers with what the window was, what it now is, and what happens at the end of it, so relay that rather than saying it was changed. | to see what is kept and how big it has grown, which is `autonomy_read`; to run the nightly sweep now, which is `pipeline_run_stage`; to change what a sweep does to a file, or to give a window to something that has none, both of which are the code's and not a setting. |
| `return_note_read` | Say what changed since the operator was last here. | Use when the operator asks what happened, what shipped, what broke or what you got done while they were away, on any surface. Returns what shipped and the check that proved it, what failed and why, what is waiting on them, what was learned, what it spent and what is still broken, every line naming the record it came from. | for a single day's summary, use `brief_read`. This answers a span since they were last here, which is usually longer than a day. |
| `session_continue` | Carry the work into a fresh start, or finish with this conversation. | Use when you have decided this conversation should end, on the grounds OPERATING.md gives for each answer. The call records what you decided; the runtime carries it out once the turn is over, so finish what you are saying first. | for a conversation you have not decided to end, which needs no call at all; to find out how full it is, which is `context_read`; to change when conversations fold from now on, which is `context_set` and is a lasting setting rather than a decision about this one; to save a single fact, which is `memory_save` and costs nothing. |
| `system_diagnose` | Report this machine's runtime health in one call. | Use to check GPU/CUDA, Ollama reachability and installed models, provider probes, open circuit breakers, scheduler job runs, and free disk. Read-only, local only, no billable calls. | for behavioural drift rather than machine health, use `conscience_status` instead; for whether the runtime's own departments need the operator, which is the Health room of the autonomy panel and a different question from whether this machine is well, use `autonomy_read`. |
| `workspace_hold` | Says which of the operator's own documents a change must be asked about, and changes that. | Use when the operator wants one of their documents held back from unattended editing, or let go again, or wants to know which ones are held now. Call it with no arguments to read the list. It answers with every document and what a change to it does, so relay that rather than saying it was changed. | to propose a change to one of those documents, which is `propose_change`; to settle a change already waiting, which is `workspace_decide`; to change the security mode, which is not a setting a tool reaches. |
| `workspace_pending` | List what is waiting on the operator to decide. | Use when the operator asks what needs them, what is waiting, whether anything wants approving, or before telling them there is nothing to do. Read it out with the id beside each one, because deciding needs the id. | for how the runtime itself is doing, which is `autonomy_read`; for this machine's health, which is `system_diagnose`. |

## Finding a tool

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `tool_search` | Make a tool callable that is not in this turn's schema. | Most tools are not in this turn's schema. They still exist. Your tool map names every one, so name the ones you want and they become callable for the rest of the session. Several at once is fine. Use plain words only when you do not know the name. | a tool already visible in this turn's schema needs no search. Call it directly. |

## Finding a playbook

| Tool | What it does | Use it when | Not for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `playbook_judge` | Keep a playbook or drop it, on the operator's word. | Use when the operator says a playbook is worth keeping or is not worth having. Keeping one activates it and carries it on every turn. Dropping one retires it, so nothing reads it again. | to read a playbook, use `playbook_search`; to write one, use `skill_create`; to reword one that is staying, use `skill_refine`. Never call this on your own account: the point of it is that the verdict came from somebody other than whoever did the work. |
| `playbook_record` | How often each playbook was used, how those turns went, and what they cost. | Use when the operator asks how a playbook is doing, whether one is worth keeping, or which of them are being carried and never read. Read this before asking for a verdict with `playbook_judge`, so the decision is made on the numbers rather than on an impression. | to read what a playbook says, use `playbook_search`. To act on the answer, use `playbook_judge`. This one only reports. |
| `playbook_search` | Read the whole of a playbook the turn is carrying only as a line. | A playbook marked (search) in your skills list looks right for this task. Name it and you get its trigger, what must hold first, its steps and its file, then read the body before following it. Plain words work when you do not know the name. | a playbook already listed with its `use_when` is carried in full this turn. Read its `SKILL.md` with `file_read` and skip this. Use `tool_search` for a TOOL rather than a procedure. |
